items.body_md:
Today, the Charleston Gazette-Mail reported that Omnis Pleasants CEO David Hindman confirmed an active sale process targeting a buyer who would acquire the 1,278-megawatt Pleasants Power Station 
"as a coal-fired plant and be able to run it for the foreseeable future,"
 the clearest public statement yet from incumbent management on the shape of the proposed transaction. The report arrives three days before the August 28 objection deadline on the Omnis Fuel Technologies / Quantum Pleasants dismissal and trustee motion (Dkt. 93), and it frames the competing narratives heading into the September 3 final hearing complex. 
Omnis Fuel Technologies filed its August 14 request for the Delaware bankruptcy court to dismiss the case or, alternatively, appoint an independent Chapter 11 trustee to replace incumbent management and investigate the attempted debt repayment and proposed sale process.
 The sale-process confirmation by Hindman is the debtor's clearest public counter to the dismissal argument that the filing served no legitimate reorganization purpose — establishing that a buyer-side process is underway is directly relevant to the good-faith inquiry under § 1112(b).

The docket on August 25 produced a rescheduled hearing notice (Dkt. 160) and a Certification of Counsel (Dkt. 161), alongside three affidavits of service (Dkts. 162–164). The Certification of Counsel is the more consequential entry: under standard Delaware practice, a Certification of Counsel is filed when counsel represents that an order has been circulated, comments have been resolved, and the court may enter the order on the papers without a hearing. Filed at this juncture — with the September 3 final hearing on cash collateral, wages, utilities, and critical vendor payments now eight days out — it likely relates to one of the uncontested first-day relief tracks, though the docket face does not identify the underlying motion. The rescheduled hearing notice (Dkt. 160) is procedural but operationally material: any shift in hearing dates in a case with this many converging deadlines can compress or relieve the September 3 timeline for one or more of the pending tracks. Neither entry alters the substantive case trajectory on its own.

The governance dispute between incumbent management (TRAG LLC and RG Energy LLC as secured lenders) and the Omnis Fuel Technologies / Quantum Pleasants bloc remains the determinative variable for recovery. 
Omnis Fuel Technologies has alleged that Quantum countered its arguments by claiming its defenses "essentially had nothing to do with" Omnis Pleasants and pertained only to Quantum.
 For the West Virginia Economic Development Authority — the debtor's largest creditor at more than $50.8 million — the August 28 dismissal objection will be the first substantive public indicator of the debtor's legal theory for preserving the case and the sale process that is the WVEDA's primary path to recovery. The next concrete milestone remains August 28, the objection deadline on Dkt. 93.

items.body_md:
On August 21, the Omnis Pleasants docket recorded a second wave of subpoenas — Dkts. 145 through 148 and 152 through 158, twelve in total — alongside two Chapter 11 first-day motion filings (Dkts. 142 and 144), a motion to file under seal (Dkt. 143), and a notice of service (Dkt. 159). The first-day motion filings at this stage of the case are not new petitions; they are almost certainly supplemental or amended first-day motions, or motions seeking approval of additional operational relief, filed as the debtor prepares for the September 3 final hearing complex. The motion to file under seal (Dkt. 143) is substantive to the extent its underlying subject matter is substantive — which, given the timing and context, likely involves materials bearing on the dismissal motion or the cash collateral record — but the sealing request itself does not independently move the case.

The twelve new subpoenas are the more consequential development. Combined with the fifteen subpoenas filed on August 20 (Dkts. 118–132, covered in Friday's briefing), the docket now reflects twenty-seven third-party subpoenas issued in a two-day window. That volume, compressed into 48 hours immediately before the August 28 objection deadline on the dismissal and trustee motion (Dkt. 93), is consistent with one or both sides conducting an accelerated pre-hearing discovery sweep keyed to the September 3 evidentiary proceedings. 
The August 14 motion filed by Omnis Fuel Technologies, LLC and Quantum Pleasants, LLC asks the court — if it declines dismissal — to appoint an independent Chapter 11 trustee and to vacate the interim cash collateral order.
 Third-party subpoenas at this stage would logically target witnesses with knowledge of the corporate authorization of the bankruptcy filing, the governance events of late July, and the circumstances surrounding the rejected $75.64 million payoff. The return dates on the subpoenas are not visible on the docket face but are presumably calibrated to produce documents and testimony before September 3.


The debtor is operating under interim cash-collateral authority while pursuing a sale of substantially all assets, with final approval set for September 3; the interim order (Dkt. 50) permits use of prepetition collateral under an approved budget, grants TRAG LLC and RG Energy LLC adequate protection, requires the debtor to continue the sale process, and limits any plan absent secured-party consent to one that pays those obligations in full in cash.
 That framework is directly in the crosshairs: a successful dismissal motion ends the case; a trustee appointment restructures who controls the sale. For unsecured creditors — including the West Virginia Economic Development Authority, 
Omnis Pleasants' largest creditor at more than $50.8 million, listed as unsecured
 — the outcome of the September 3 hearing complex is the central recovery variable. The debtor's Young Conaway and Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer teams are now simultaneously managing objections to a subpoena barrage, briefing the dismissal opposition due August 28, and preparing final-hearing submissions on wages, utilities, critical vendor payments, and cash collateral — all converging on a single hearing date. The next concrete milestone is August 28, the objection deadline on the dismissal and trustee motion (Dkt. 93), which will be the first substantive public indicator of the debtor's legal theory for why the case should survive.

items.lede: On August 20, fifteen subpoenas — Dkts. 118 through 132 — landed on the Omnis Pleasants docket in a single day.
items.body_md:
On August 20, fifteen subpoenas — Dkts. 118 through 132 — landed on the Omnis Pleasants docket in a single day. The docket lines are captioned uniformly as "Subpoena," with no further description of recipients or subject matter visible on their face. Fifteen subpoenas filed simultaneously is not a routine discovery event, even in a contested Chapter 11. The timing and volume place this squarely in the context of the dismissal motion (Dkt. 93) filed by Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum Pleasants: with the objection deadline on that motion set for August 28 and the September 3 final cash collateral and first-day hearings closing in, either the movants or the debtor — most likely the movants given the aggressive posture Lowenstein Sandler has already established through the First Set of Requests for Production (Dkt. 99) — is moving to lock in third-party testimony and document production before the contested hearings. Discovery in support of a dismissal motion or a trustee-appointment request would logically target individuals with knowledge of the circumstances surrounding the Chapter 11 filing itself: the corporate authorization question, the rejected $75.64 million payoff, the governance dispute, and the events preceding the West Virginia state court loss one business day before the petition date.

The practical consequence for the debtor is compounding pressure. The estate is now simultaneously defending against a dismissal/trustee motion with a hard August 28 objection deadline, managing third-party document production in response to Dkt. 99, responding to fifteen subpoenas whose return dates are unknown from the docket face but are presumably keyed to the September 3 hearing complex, and preparing final-hearing submissions on cash collateral and first-day operational orders. Each of those tracks feeds into the others: if subpoena responses surface evidence bearing on corporate authority or the circumstances of the filing, that evidence reaches the dismissal hearing; if the dismissal motion carries, the cash collateral and first-day orders become moot. The debtor's counsel at Young Conaway and Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer will need to manage objections to any subpoenas that are overbroad or seek privileged material while simultaneously briefing the substantive response to Dkt. 93 — a resource allocation problem that is not trivial.

For creditors and claimants, the subpoena barrage is the clearest indicator yet that the August 28 and September 3 proceedings are heading toward full-scale evidentiary contests rather than uncontested hearings. 
The debtor is operating under interim cash-collateral authority while pursuing a sale of substantially all assets, with the final approval of that authority set for September 3; the interim cash-collateral order requires the debtor to continue the sale process and limits any plan absent secured-party consent to one that pays TRAG LLC and RG Energy LLC in full in cash.
 A contested dismissal that succeeds, or a trustee appointment in the alternative, would fundamentally reset those dynamics: a Chapter 11 trustee would step into control of the sale process and could take positions adverse to the debtor's current secured-party relationships. 
If the court declines dismissal, the movants are asking it to appoint an independent Chapter 11 trustee and to vacate the interim cash collateral order.
 Recovery posture for unsecured creditors, including the West Virginia Economic Development Authority — 
the largest creditor at more than $50.8 million, listed as unsecured
 — depends heavily on whether the sale process proceeds on the debtor's terms or is restructured under a trustee. The next concrete milestone is August 27, the objection deadline on the professional retention applications (including Sidley Austin as special regulatory counsel, Dkt. 85), followed by August 28, the objection deadline on the dismissal and trustee motion (Dkt. 93).

items.body_md:
On August 18, Omnis Pleasants filed Dkt. 100, extending the objection deadline on its cash collateral motion (related to Dkts. 17 and 50) — the interim order authorizing postpetition use of prepetition collateral, adequate protection to TRAG LLC and RG Energy LLC, automatic stay modification, and related relief. The extension notice was filed as an exhibit, and the docket entry does not specify the new deadline on its face; the materiality here is procedural-but-important: the cash collateral final hearing remains anchored to September 3, but the objection window has now been formally extended, likely to accommodate the contested posture created by the dismissal motion (Dkt. 93). Any party opposing the final cash collateral order — most obviously Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum Pleasants — gains additional runway to file that objection in coordination with their August 28 dismissal opposition deadline. Dkt. 101 is the $199.00 filing fee receipt for the sale motion; it is administrative and carries no substantive weight.

The News and Sentinel's August 18 piece adds texture to the dismissal motion's theory without moving the docket. 
The motion raises an unusual structural argument: according to Omnis Fuel Technologies, the TRAG/RGE loans were made principally to parent or affiliated companies, and Omnis Pleasants itself is neither a borrower nor a guarantor of those obligations
 — yet TRAG and RG Energy assert security interests against the plant's assets. 
The movants argue that Chapter 11 is being used to resolve a financing and control dispute involving parties above the operating company rather than to restructure the debts of a financially distressed power station
. If that theory holds, it would undercut the debtor's primary justification for the filing and — critically — the premise on which the interim cash collateral order was granted, since that order was predicated on the validity of the secured parties' prepetition claims against estate property. The debtor's response to the dismissal motion, due August 28, will need to address the borrower/guarantor point directly; a failure to rebut it credibly risks the court questioning whether the automatic stay should remain in place at all.

The discovery posture from the First Set of Requests for Production (Dkt. 99, served August 17 by Lowenstein Sandler on behalf of Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum Pleasants) continues to run concurrently with all of the above. The debtor faces simultaneous obligations: briefing the dismissal opposition, managing document production, and preparing for the September 3 final hearings on cash collateral and first-day operational orders. The extended objection deadline on the cash collateral motion (Dkt. 100) sharpens the convergence — if an objection lands from Omnis Fuel Technologies on the eve of the final hearing, the court may face a contested cash collateral confirmation at the same September 3 session already carrying the dismissal motion's shadow. The next hard milestone is August 27, objection deadline on the five professional retention applications (including Sidley Austin as special regulatory counsel, Dkt. 85), followed by August 28, objection deadline on the dismissal/trustee motion (Dkt. 93).

That clears the path for Judge Owens to enter a final order on taxes and fees without further hearing, consistent with the interim order's own terms. The practical effect is modest but tidy: one discrete first-day item moves toward closure, and the September 3 final hearing agenda loses a contested line item it never had. Dkt. 100, filed August 18 as an exhibit, carries no standalone docket description identifying the underlying motion or adversary proceeding it supports; its materiality depends on that attachment context, which the docket entry alone does not resolve.

The more consequential frame for today remains the dismissal motion (Dkt. 93) and the discovery posture built around it. 
Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum Pleasants filed their dismissal motion on August 14, supported by the Gassenheimer declaration (Dkt. 94), asking the court in the alternative to appoint a Chapter 11 trustee and to vacate the Interim Cash Collateral Order.
 
The motion asserts that Pleasants had approximately $13 million in liquidity when the petition was filed and was cash-flow positive
 — the factual predicate the First Set of Requests for Production (Dkt. 99) is plainly designed to test or reinforce from the debtor's own documents. The debtor's objection deadline on the dismissal motion is August 28, and the RFP issued by Lowenstein Sandler on August 17 runs concurrently, meaning the debtor is simultaneously preparing an opposition brief and managing a document production obligation under the same ten-day compression. A motion for protective order, if the debtor elects to resist discovery, would itself consume time and judge's attention in advance of the September 3 cluster.


The debtor is operating under interim cash-collateral authority conditioned on continuing the sale process; the interim order requires that any plan absent secured-party consent pay TRAG LLC and RG Energy LLC in full in cash.
 Dismissal or trustee appointment would disrupt that sale track entirely, which is the central recovery risk for unsecured creditors — including the West Virginia Economic Development Authority's approximately $50.9 million unsecured claim. The next hard milestone is August 27 (objection deadline on the five professional retention applications, including Sidley Austin as special regulatory counsel, Dkt. 85), followed by August 28 (objection deadline on the dismissal/trustee motion, Dkt. 93), and then the September 2 Section 341 meeting and the September 3 final hearings on cash collateral, first-day operational orders, and professional retentions.

items.body_md:
On August 17, Omnis Fuel Technologies, LLC and Quantum Pleasants, LLC served the debtor with a First Set of Requests for Production (Dkt. 99), filed by Christopher Ward of Lowenstein Sandler LLP — the same firm that secured pro hac vice admission for Michael A. Kaplan and Rebecca J. Ryan on the same date (Dkts. 95–98). The RFP service is the first formal discovery move in the case and is substantively important in context: Lowenstein Sandler's entry, concurrent with the dismissal motion filed August 14 (Dkt. 93), signals that Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum Pleasants are building a litigation record in support of their bad-faith/no-authority theory, not merely pressing a pleading. Discovery directed at the debtor in connection with a dismissal motion is irregular — such motions are typically decided on the pleadings and existing record — and its issuance suggests the movants either anticipate an evidentiary hearing before Judge Owens or are laying groundwork for one by forcing document production before the August 28 objection deadline on Dkt. 93. Dkts. 95–98 (the pro hac vice motions and orders for Kaplan and Ryan) are procedural and routine.

The practical effect for the debtor is immediate: a discovery obligation now runs in parallel with its obligation to file an objection to the dismissal/trustee motion by August 28. The debtor will need to decide whether to move for a protective order or comply, and any delay in the sale marketing process attributable to discovery litigation could compress Houlihan Lokey's runway before the September 3 final cash collateral hearing. For creditors — particularly the West Virginia Economic Development Authority, holding an unsecured claim of approximately $50.9 million — the introduction of formal discovery into what was nominally a dismissal motion raises the stakes of that hearing materially. If the movants use the RFP responses to sharpen the evidentiary case for bad faith, the debtor's opposition will need to be more than a legal brief: it will need to address factual record developed from its own documents. The alternative interpretation — that the RFP is tactical pressure rather than a genuine evidentiary project — is also plausible, but the simultaneous admission of two Lowenstein Sandler partners with specialized litigation backgrounds is more consistent with a coordinated discovery-and-briefing strategy than with a motion the movants expect to win on the papers alone.

Tomorrow, August 19, is the objection deadline on the prepetition taxes and fees interim order (Dkt. 49, capped at $775,000). No objections have appeared on the docket as of today; if none are filed by 4:00 p.m. Eastern, the court may enter the final order without a further hearing. The next hard deadline after that is August 27 (objections to the five professional retention applications, Dkts. 81–85), followed by August 28 (objections to the dismissal/trustee motion, Dkt. 93), with the September 3 final hearings on cash collateral, first-day orders, and professional retentions — and the Section 341 meeting of creditors on September 2 — constituting the case's next inflection cluster.

items.body_md:
On August 14, Omnis Fuel Technologies, LLC d/b/a Omnis Energy and Quantum Pleasants, LLC filed Dkt. 93, a motion seeking, in the alternative: (I) outright dismissal of the Chapter 11 case as a bad-faith filing, (II) appointment of a Chapter 11 trustee, and (III) vacatur of the interim cash collateral order — the most direct attack yet on the legitimacy of the case and the authority of current management. The motion was accompanied by the declaration of Charles Gassenheimer (Dkt. 94), president of Omnis Fuel Technologies, whose core thesis — developed in prior filings and now formalized as a standalone dismissal motion — is that 
Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum Pleasants contend that the July 16, 2026 payment to TRAG LLC and RG Energy LLC terminated the forbearance agreement that empowered independent manager Gilbert Nathan, and that the debtor lacked authority to file the case once they installed Gassenheimer as interim director.
 
Gassenheimer's position, stated in his declaration, is that "upon Payment in Full of all Obligations, the Forbearance Agreement and underlying loan agreements terminate automatically by their own terms, all liens are released, and the governance restrictions — including the Independent Manager structure — cease."
 The motion is triply structured: dismissal for want of authority and bad faith is the primary ask; trustee appointment is the fallback if the court declines to dismiss; and vacatur of the interim cash collateral order is the third prong, which, if granted, would halt the debtor's ability to operate pending any further hearing. Objections are due August 28, 2026. The September 3 final cash collateral hearing is now squarely in the crosshairs of this motion, as the movants are asking the court to eliminate the interim order that is the foundation of the debtor's operating authority between now and that date.

The legal and factual contest at the core of this motion is the same one that has animated the case since the petition date, but the procedural posture has now shifted materially. 
The interim cash collateral order authorized use of collateral through the scheduled final hearing without resolving the objectors' underlying challenge to the debtor's authority to file the case or their request to dismiss it
 — that deferral is now over. 
The July 16 payment was an uncertified check for $75.64 million delivered by entities including Dynamic Finance Corporation, asserting full satisfaction of the loans; Nathan rejected the transaction after the payor and source of funds went undisclosed.
 
On July 21, TRAG/RG Energy filed counterclaims and a TRO in the West Virginia action seeking to maintain Nathan as independent manager; the West Virginia court denied that TRO on July 24.
 The movants' bad-faith theory therefore rests on three linked propositions: that the payment legally terminated the forbearance agreement, that Nathan's subsequent removal was valid, and that current management accordingly lacked authority to authorize the bankruptcy filing. The debtor, for its part, has consistently taken the position that the payment was properly rejected and that Nathan remained the independent manager at the time of filing. Judge Owens has not ruled on the authority question, and the August 28 objection deadline and the September 3 hearing will force that question to a head. For creditors, the stakes could not be higher: a dismissal would extinguish the § 363 sale process and the automatic stay simultaneously, exposing the estate to a race among creditors outside the protection of the Code.

Also confirmed by the August 13 docket entries are the identities of the debtor's proposed professionals across Dkts. 81–85: AP Services, LLC (designating David Hindman as CEO, Dkt. 81); Young Conaway Stargatt & Taylor, LLP as co-counsel (Dkt. 82); Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer (US) LLP as lead debtor's counsel (Dkt. 83); Houlihan Lokey Capital, Inc. as investment banker effective August 3, 2026 (Dkt. 84); and Sidley Austin LLP as special regulatory counsel (Dkt. 85). Houlihan Lokey's engagement is the most creditor-relevant of these: it signals that the sale marketing process is being run by a national energy M&A practice, and objection deadline for all five is August 27, 2026, with hearings set for September 3. 
The interim cash collateral order requires the debtor to continue the sale process and limits any plan, absent the secured parties' consent, to one that pays their obligations in full in cash
 — a constraint that makes Houlihan Lokey's mandate structurally central to whatever recovery unsecured creditors can realistically expect. RG Energy and TRAG also admitted three additional outside counsel pro hac vice (Dkts. 87–92: Dale K. Cathell, Jeffrey S. Torosian, Jonathan M. Kinney), which in context of the simultaneously filed dismissal motion signals a coordinated litigation team now in place on both the dismissal front and the September 3 hearing. The next hard deadlines are August 19 (objections to the prepetition tax order, Dkt. 49), August 27 (objections to the five professional retentions), August 28 (objections to the dismissal/trustee motion, Dkt. 93), and September 3 (final hearings on cash collateral, first-day orders, and professional retentions).

items.body_md:
On August 13, the debtor filed a motion to establish notice and procedures for the assumption and assignment of contracts and leases (Dkt. 86), the most consequential filing of this cycle given that a § 363 sale of the Pleasants Power Station is the stated exit path. An assumption-and-assignment procedures motion governs the mechanics by which the estate identifies executory contracts and unexpired leases it intends to transfer to a buyer — including cure-notice timelines, the process for counterparties to object to cure amounts or adequate assurance, and the deadline structure that will govern any sale closing. In a 1,278-MW coal-fired generation asset operating within PJM and carrying a counterparty roster that includes energy trading arrangements and PJM-related obligations, the universe of contracts subject to § 365 treatment is substantial, and the procedures order will set the objection and cure-dispute framework that counterparties and the estate must navigate before any § 363 sale closes. The content of Dkt. 86 is not fully reproduced in available record; the identity of any proposed stalking-horse bidder, cure-estimate methodology, or deadline structure will require a full-text pull and will be reported when confirmed.

Also filed August 13 were five additional employment and retention applications (Dkts. 81–85), beyond the Stretto administrative advisor application (Dkt. 79) and the interim compensation procedures motion (Dkt. 78) covered in yesterday's briefing. The identities of the five proposed professionals are not confirmed from available docket text and are unverified here; what confirmation looks like is the full-text pull of each application. As a cluster, they are substantive filings — each draws on estate resources and defines who bills the estate — but absent any indication of contest, they are routine at this stage of a Chapter 11. If any of the five engages a financial advisor, investment banker, or restructuring advisor with a sale mandate, that appointment would carry material weight for creditor recovery and will be elevated when confirmed. Dkts. 87–92, filed today, are pro hac vice motions and admissions for additional counsel — procedural and routine, requiring no further analysis.

The August 19 objection deadline for final approval of the prepetition tax order (Dkt. 49, authorizing up to $775,000 in prepetition tax and fee payments) remains the nearest hard date, now five days out, with no objection on the docket as of this briefing. The next concrete milestones are August 19 (tax-order objection deadline), September 2 (§ 341(a) meeting of creditors, 1:00 p.m. ET via Zoom), and September 3 (final hearings on wages, utility payments, and critical vendor orders). Dkt. 86's assumption-and-assignment procedures motion will require a hearing date; none is confirmed on the record, and the timing of that hearing relative to any § 363 sale motion will be the next structural question to watch.

items.body_md:
On August 12, McDermott Will & Schulte LLP filed a Notice of Withdrawal of Appearance (Dkt. 73), exiting the case entirely on behalf of TRAG LLC and RG Energy LLC — the first-lien creditors whose $87.3 million lien position defines the secured layer of this capital structure. The withdrawal is the substantive event of the past 24 hours and warrants attention. As recently as August 7, McDermott Will & Schulte had admitted two partners pro hac vice (Dkts. 69-72), making the exit unusually abrupt: two admissions and a notice of appearance, all reversed within five days. No substitute counsel has appeared on behalf of TRAG or RG Energy as of this writing. 
TRAG LLC and RG Energy LLC, both connected to investor Tony Robbins, hold liens and security interests granted at the end of June in the amount of $87.3 million.
 That position gives them leverage over essentially every outcome in this case — plan confirmation, any § 363 sale process, and cash-collateral use — making their counsel posture directly relevant to recovery prospects for the broader creditor body.

The practical consequences of an unrepresented first-lien creditor are immediate. Without active counsel of record, TRAG and RG Energy cannot file an objection, respond to a motion, or participate at the September 3 final hearing on the first-day critical operations orders — wages, utilities, and critical vendor payments — without first securing replacement representation and moving that new counsel through admission. The objection deadline for those final orders is August 19, six days out. If no new counsel appears before then, the entities most capable of contesting the final first-day relief lose their standing to do so. Whether the withdrawal reflects a strategic decision by TRAG/RG Energy to allow the operational orders to pass uncontested, a breakdown in the client-counsel relationship, or a transition to different outside counsel not yet announced is unknown on the current record. None of those readings is verifiable from the docket alone, and reasonable observers could disagree on which is most plausible. Dkts. 74, 75, and 76 — the U.S. Trustee's scheduling request, Zoom logistics notice, and formal Notice of Meeting of Creditors — set the § 341(a) meeting for September 2, 2026 at 1:00 p.m. ET, with a § 523 dischargeability objection deadline of November 2, 2026. Those filings are administrative infrastructure; they are noted for timing but carry no independent bearing on creditor recovery.

The next hard deadline is August 19 — objections to the final orders on wages, utilities, and taxes are due at 4:00 p.m. ET per Dkt. 49. The absence of counsel for TRAG and RG Energy against that deadline is the position to watch. The September 2 § 341(a) meeting follows, and the September 3 final hearings on the first-day operational orders are the next substantive event on the calendar.

items.body_md:
On August 7, four attorneys filed notices and motions to appear in Case No. 26-11169 before Judge Karen Owens in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, with two pro hac vice admissions granted (Dkt. 71–72) and two motions pending (Dkt. 69–70), accompanied by a notice of appearance (Dkt. 68). The cluster of new entrants — five docket entries in a single day — signals that additional parties, beyond Industrial Accessories Company (which appeared July 31 via Dkt. 60) and Kuro Infrastructure Delaware, Inc. (whose counsel was admitted pro hac vice July 31, Dkt. 59), are now formally inserting themselves into the proceeding. The identities of those counsel are not disclosed on the face of the docket entries available; confirmation of who they represent will appear on the underlying appearance pleadings, which should be treated as the primary source once accessible.

That said, the directional read matters for recovery posture. 
As of the petition date, the debtor carried prepetition funded debt and guarantee obligations of approximately $70.8 million, comprising the approximately $50.9 million unsecured WVEDA loan guarantee (matured June 2026 and in default) and a purported $20 million unsecured Bilt note (in payment default), alongside a first-priority lien on substantially all of the debtor's assets granted to TRAG/RGE to secure more than $80 million of loans made to the debtor's non-debtor parent entities.
 With no unsecured creditors' committee yet appointed — confirmed by Dkt. 66 filed August 4 — the arrival of new appearing parties is the primary mechanism by which creditor constituencies are currently self-organizing. 
The debtor has stated it intends to investigate and prosecute estate claims against former management for the benefit of stakeholders,
 and the governance dispute between the Gassheimer/Quantum Pleasants faction and incumbent management — including 
Dynamic Finance Corp.'s delivery of a $75.64 million check purporting to fulfill all obligations under loan documents
 — remains unresolved on the docket. Creditors tracking recovery should monitor whether any newly appearing party has a nexus to either the TRAG/RGE lien position or the contested governance narrative, as that would materially affect whether the section 363 sale process runs cleanly or faces competing bids for control.

The procedural move for the week is straightforward: the docket is in its early-stage coalition-formation phase. 
Young Conaway Stargatt & Taylor LLP and Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer LLP are representing Omnis Pleasants LLC
 on the debtor side, and the next concrete milestone is the September 3 final hearing on the first-day critical operations orders covering employee wages, utility payments, and critical vendor payments — the session at which interim relief approved at the outset of the case will either be made permanent or modified.

Friday's five docket entries — Dkt. 68 through 72, plus an attorney-addition event — consist entirely of two pro hac vice motions (Dkt. 69, 70), their corresponding admission orders (Dkt. 71, 72), and a notice of appearance (Dkt. 68), all filed August 7.
items.body_md:
The 72-hour lookback window through August 8 is thin. Friday's five docket entries — Dkt. 68 through 72, plus an attorney-addition event — consist entirely of two pro hac vice motions (Dkt. 69, 70), their corresponding admission orders (Dkt. 71, 72), and a notice of appearance (Dkt. 68), all filed August 7. Yesterday's briefing flagged these filings and noted the identities of the admitting attorneys and their clients as unverified from the ground truth alone. That remains true today: no primary-source motion papers have been surfaced to confirm who entered the case. The pattern itself — a paired cluster of pro hac vice admissions arriving on a Friday, roughly three weeks into an active Chapter 11 — warrants continued attention, but absent confirmed identities it carries no actionable implication for the recovery posture.

No new press coverage dated August 8 has emerged. The most recent secondary reporting remains the August 5 Herald-Dispatch and Charleston Gazette-Mail articles already covered. Those pieces added regional texture to the governance fight — specifically, 
Gassheimer's account that TRAG/RGE filed counterclaims and a TRO motion in the West Virginia action on July 21 seeking to restore Nathan as Independent Manager, and that the West Virginia court denied that TRO on July 24
 — and they confirm that the Hindman management team has characterized 
the $75.6 million Dynamic Finance check as "uncertified," rejected for lack of transparency regarding the source of funds
. Neither development is new to the Delaware docket; they are factual anchors for the governance contest whose resolution, or escalation, will shape the August 19 objection period. One additional data point from regional coverage that has not been fully absorbed: 
prior management entered into a power purchase agreement in December 2025 with Element H, an affiliate owned by the Hodson family, at prices alleged to be below the cost of generation, with potential losses cited at $1 billion
 — __[News and Sentinel](https://www.newsandsentinel.com/news/business/2026/08/power-struggle-new-pleasants-power-leadership-fights-with-former-management-in-bankruptcy-filings/)__. That allegation is unverified (it appears in Hindman's declaration, not in a court ruling), but if substantiated it would materially widen the universe of potential estate claims and, by extension, the recovery pool available to unsecured creditors including the WVEDA.

Today's concrete task is a factual one: confirm from the underlying motion papers the identities of the counsel and parties behind Dkt. 69–72. Until those are known, the significance of Friday's appearance cluster — whether it represents a significant creditor, an adverse party organizing into the governance dispute, or a potential § 363 bidder — cannot be assessed. The next hard milestone is August 19, 2026, the objection deadline for the first-day operational orders set by Dkt. 57, followed by the September 3 final hearing before Judge Karen Owens in Courtroom 3, 824 Market Street, Wilmington, at 1:00 PM.
